subject: system-design
title: Distributed Monitoring
summary: Watching the health of a large fleet: collecting metrics into a time-series database, visualizing them on dashboards, and alerting on the symptoms users actually feel.

blocks.text: Monitoring is how you know whether a large system is healthy without watching every machine by hand. Each host and service emits metrics, which are numbers like request rate, error count, and CPU use. A monitoring system gathers, stores, and surfaces them so you can spot trouble before users do.

There are two ways to gather metrics. In the pull model, the monitoring server scrapes a metrics endpoint each service exposes, on a schedule. This is how Prometheus works, and it makes service discovery and health implicit. In the push model, services send metrics to a collector themselves, which suits short-lived jobs that may be gone before a scrape. Many fleets use both.

Metrics are timestamped numbers, so they live in a time-series database optimized for that shape: heavy append, range queries by time, and aggregation across many series. Dashboards (commonly Grafana) then aggregate and chart those series so a human can read the fleet's state at a glance and zoom into a specific window when something looks off.

items: Latency: how long requests take. Track failed-request latency separately.
Traffic: how much demand the system is under, like requests per second.
Errors: the rate of requests that fail, explicitly or implicitly.
Saturation: how full the system is, meaning the resource closest to its limit.

blocks.text: Dashboards need someone watching; alerts come to you. Rules fire when a metric crosses a threshold or deviates from its normal pattern (anomaly detection), routing a notification to whoever is on call. Good alerts are actionable. They point at a problem a human can and should do something about right now.

blocks.title: Beware alert fatigue
blocks.text: Alert on symptoms users feel, such as high latency or an elevated error rate, not on every internal metric. A flood of noisy, non-actionable alerts trains responders to ignore them, so the one alert that matters gets missed.

Server-side monitoring sees what your infrastructure does, but it is blind to failures that never reach the server, such as a broken CDN edge, a client crash, or a flaky last-mile network. Client-side or real-user monitoring reports from the user's device, capturing the experience the server can't observe. You need both to know the system is truly healthy for the people using it.
